accepted.reason: Best observation-target alignment: hospitalization rates plausibly lag an infection proxy, and delayed_I is explicitly recommended. SEIR with a fixed delay is parsimonious for a short (31-week) single-season, high-peakiness series and avoids adding a potentially weakly identifiable H compartment.

Same strong alignment (delayed_I) and low complexity as proposal 0, while probing a nearby lag value. Given uncertainty in admission/reporting lag by age group, a 1-week alternative is reasonable without increasing identifiability risk.

Also matches recommended delayed_I mapping and keeps dynamics simple. A 3-week lag is still within a plausible range to test phase sensitivity without introducing extra compartments or fractional memory.

rejected.reason: Observation-target misalignment risk: using contemporaneous I for a hospitalization-rate target contradicts the stated surveillance semantics that admissions may lag I. With high peakiness, even small phase errors can dominate, so this control is likely to be systematically biased in timing rather than informative.

suggested_edits.edit: Clarify that delay_weeks is an integer-week approximation to an underlying continuous lag; note that fixed-delay assumption may be strained near peak but is retained to avoid over-parameterization in a 31-week single-season series.
Add a brief note that 1-week delay is primarily a sensitivity check for earlier peak alignment; keep all other components identical to proposal 0 to preserve identifiability.
Add a caution that 3-week delay may be less plausible for short, sharp peaks; frame it explicitly as a boundary/sensitivity case rather than a primary hypothesis.
If retained as a diagnostic, consider switching observation_map from I to delayed_I with delay_weeks=0 to keep semantics consistent while still testing the no-lag hypothesis.
